headline: High risk of filesystem-based prompt injection and data leakage from Claude Code into Great Expectations; default shared-workspace use is unsafe.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A reads and writes repo files and shares state via filesystem/git; agent B consumes files for validation results and documentation. That creates a plausible file-content injection path even though no direct parser behavior is documented. Because both profiles expose shared files, the interaction exists in default workflows and uncertainty pushes above low.
conditions: IF agent A writes attacker-controlled instructions into a file that agent B later parses as configuration or documentation, injection is possible.
IF both agents operate in the same workspace without file provenance checks, file-based instruction smuggling remains possible.
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent.
Require explicit allowlists for files B may read.
Add a provenance header check before B consumes A-written files.
Use read-only mounts for B where feasible.
requires-engineering: add content-signing or checksum verification between agents.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent A touches source code, git history, shell environment, and files in cwd, while agent B reads data sources, validation results, and documentation. Shared filesystem access means sensitive repo or environment data can flow from A into B outputs. B is local-only by profile, so this is not high, but the shared workspace makes leakage plausible in default use.
conditions: IF agent A has access to secrets or proprietary code in the workspace, and agent B reads those files, leakage can occur.
IF B is pointed at the same directory tree as A, validation outputs may expose A-read content.
mitigations: Use separate directories for sensitive and non-sensitive data.
Mask secrets before B reads any files.
Restrict B to a curated input manifest.
Review B outputs for accidental echoing of source content.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent access controls at the filesystem layer.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Agent A can write the filesystem, modify git state, and use broad network egress; agent B can install packages and read/write files in data workflows. Overlap on mutable files and package state creates conflict risk, though B lacks network egress so the blast radius is narrower than high. No locking is documented, so concurrent edits remain plausible.
conditions: IF both agents modify the same git branch or working tree concurrently, conflicts can corrupt state.
IF agent A installs or updates packages while B depends on the same environment, dependency drift can occur.
mitigations: Serialize writes to the repo.
Pin dependencies before either agent runs.
Use separate virtual environments.
Pause one agent during git operations by the other.
requires-engineering: add file and git locks in the orchestrator.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent A can generate code or file changes that agent B may treat as validation inputs or documentation artifacts. B is a data-quality tool, so it may operationalize A's outputs without independent semantic verification. That is a default workflow risk, but not clearly an autonomous action-taking chain, so medium fits better than high.
conditions: IF agent B consumes A-produced files as authoritative test inputs, errors can cascade into false validation results.
IF A writes documentation or configs that B later validates without human review, incorrect assumptions can propagate.
mitigations: Insert a human review step between A and B.
Require B to validate against source-of-truth inputs only.
Tag A-generated artifacts as untrusted.
Compare B outputs against a baseline before acting.
requires-engineering: add schema validation and provenance tracking.

E_compliance.rationale: No explicit residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented for either agent. Agent A handles git credentials and source code; agent B handles validation results and documentation. Because the profiles do not show a concrete compliance divergence, only a limited overlap exists and the other agent is not separately cited beyond its data classes.
conditions: IF regulated data such as PHI or EU PII is introduced into the shared workspace, a compliance review is required.
IF retention or residency requirements differ between the two deployment environments, policy mismatch may arise.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the shared workspace.
Document retention settings for both agents.
Review whether either agent stores logs externally.
Restrict secrets to the minimum needed.
requires-engineering: align residency and retention controls before deployment.
